text: Solomon Hersh Frees (June 22, 1920 – November 2, 1986), better known as Paul Frees, was an American actor, comedian, impressionist, and vaudevillian renowned for his work on Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer, Walter Lantz, Rankin/Bass, and Walt Disney theatrical cartoons during the Golden Age of Animation, and for providing the voice of Boris Badenov in The Rocky and Bullwinkle Show. Born to a Jewish family in Chicago on June 22, 1920, he grew up in the Albany Park neighborhood and attended Von Steuben Junior High School. In the 1930s, he began performing in vaudeville as an impressionist under the name Buddy Green. He started his radio career in 1942 and remained active for over 40 years, appearing in more than 250 films, cartoons, and TV shows, often without credit. His radio career was interrupted when he was drafted into the U.S. Army during World War II, where he fought at Normandy, France, on D-Day, was wounded, and returned to the U.S. for recuperation. He attended the Chouinard Art Institute under the G.I. Bill and later returned to radio after his first wife's health declined. He frequently appeared on Hollywood radio series such as Escape, Suspense, Gunsmoke, Crime Classics, and The Green Lama, where he played lead roles and narrated in The Player. He starred as Jethro Dumont/Green Lama in The Green Lama (1949) and as Larry Mitchell on Crime Correspondent on CBS Radio. Frees dubbed Toshiro Mifune’s performance as Admiral Yamamoto in Midway, provided much of the falsetto voice for Tony Curtis’ character Josephine and the voice of funeral director Mozzarella in Some Like It Hot, and replaced Dick Wessel in the Disney film The Ugly Dachshund as Eddie, dubbing lines from Humphrey Bogart in The Harder They Fall due to Bogart’s poor vocal condition from esophageal cancer. He worked with at least nine major animation studios, including Walt Disney Productions, Warner Bros. Cartoons, Walter Lantz, UPA, Hanna-Barbera, Filmation, DePatie-Freleng, Jay Ward, Rankin/Bass, and Ruby-Spears. He voiced Professor Ludwig Von Drake in 18 episodes of the Disney anthology series beginning September 24, 1961, and narrated Donald in Mathmagic Land, which aired alongside Von Drake’s debut. He also voiced the "Ghost Host" at Disneyland and Walt Disney World, provided the ghost voice for "dead men tell no tales" in Pirates of the Caribbean, and voiced characters such as the Auctioneer, Magistrate Carlos, and the "Pooped Pirate." He narrated Adventure Thru Inner Space (1967–1985) and Great Moments with Mr. Lincoln, and audio clips from these attractions are used in Disneyland fireworks. An animated singing bust in his likeness appeared in The Haunted Mansion (2003), and audio from Pirates of the Caribbean is featured in Pirates of the Caribbean: At World's End. Frees had a small on-camera role in The Shaggy Dog (1959) as Dr. Galvin and provided the film’s opening narration. He voiced characters in numerous Disney anthology episodes and was honored posthumously as a Disney Legend on October 9, 2006. He provided voices for Boris Badenov, Inspector Fenwick, Ape, District Commissioner Alistair, Weevil Plumtree, Baron Otto Matic, Fred, and the Hoppity Hooper narrator in Jay Ward cartoons. He voiced many characters in Rankin/Bass holiday specials, including Captain Jones in The Mouse on the Mayflower (1968), the father of Drummer Boy Ali and the three Wise Men in The Little Drummer Boy (1968), Hocus Pocus, the traffic cop, ticket-taker, and Santa Claus in Frosty the Snowman (1969), and Burgermeister Meisterburger and Grimsley in Santa Claus Is Comin' to Town (1970), as well as Aeon the Terrible in Rudolph's Shiny New Year (1976). He voiced King Haggard’s wizard Mabruk and the Cat in The Last Unicorn and several voices for the Jackson Five cartoon series (1971–1973), and J.R.R. Tolkien characters, including Bombur, in Rankin/Bass adaptations of The Hobbit and The Return of the King. He portrayed an Orson Welles sound-alike in The War of the Worlds (1953), provided the apocalyptic voice for the "talking rings" in The Time Machine (1960), and did the opening narration for Atlantis, the Lost Continent (1960) and Doc Savage (1975). He narrated The Fantasy Film Worlds of George Pal (1985) and provided voices for Arnie the Dinosaur and the Pillsbury Doughboy in The Puppetoon Movie (1987). He voiced three main characters in the U.S. versions of Hergé’s Adventures of Tintin. He worked on MGM’s Tom and Jerry shorts, including Blue Cat Blues (1956), where he voiced Jerry, and Jerry’s Cousin and His Mouse Friday, and performed multiple roles in Tex Avery’s short films, notably all roles in Cellbound (1955). He appeared as "Billy Playtex" and other characters on Spike Jones’ 1960 album Omnibust. From October 1961 to September 1962, he voiced Judge Oliver Wendell Clutch, a weasel, on Calvin and the Colonel. In the 1962 Christmas special Mister Magoo's Christmas Carol, he voiced Fezziwig, the Charity Man, Eyepatch Man, Tall Tophat Man, and the Broadway theatre director, and later provided numerous voices for The Famous Adventures of Mr. Magoo. He voiced John Lennon and George Harrison in The Beatles cartoon series, served as narrator, Big D, and Fluid Man in Frankenstein Jr. and The Impossibles, The Thing in Fantastic Four (1967), and President James Norcross in Super President (1967), and played narrator, Chef of State, judges, and bailiff in Twice Upon a Time. He provided the voice-over for the trailer to Play Misty for Me (1971). In commercials, he was the voice of the Pillsbury Doughboy, 7-Up bird Fresh-Up Freddie, Froot Loops spokesbird Toucan Sam (previously voiced by Mel Blanc, later by Maurice LaMarche), Boo-Berry, and The Farmer who helps The Little Green Sprout (voiced by Ike Eisenmann), and played a British detective in a 1971 Taster's Choice coffee commercial. He narrated live-action films and series such as Naked City (1958–1963) and provided the voice of eccentric billionaire John Beresford Tipton on The Millionaire. He narrated the opening of The Disorderly Orderly and looped an actor’s voice in The Ladies Man, both starring Jerry Lewis. In 1980, he was hired as the voice of radio station WKXW (Kicks 101 1/2). Frees was known in the industry as "The Man of a Thousand Voices," though that title is more commonly associated with Mel Blanc. He was also a songwriter and screenwriter, with his most notable work being the 1959 film The Beatniks, a critique of the Beat counterculture, which was mocked on Mystery Science Theater 3000 in 1992. He appeared on-camera in films such as Suddenly (1954), The Thing from Another World, A Place in the Sun, and The Big Sky, and in episodes of The Ray Milland Show (1955) and Beginning of the End (1957). In Jet Pilot, he played a Soviet officer who ejects from a parked jet to rescue John Wayne, and narrated the opening of Rescue 8 (1958–1959). In Patton (1970), he provided voices for a war correspondent, a staff member, and a Moroccan official, and voiced the English-language Japanese ambassador in Tora! Tora! Tora! and delivered the final narration in Beneath the Planet of the Apes. After his death, Corey Burton has re-recorded dialogue for several Disneyland attractions originally recorded by Frees, due to deterioration of the original recordings or plot changes, such as the replacement of the "Pooped Pirate" with the "Stuffed Pirate" in Pirates of the Caribbean in 1997. Burton also recorded the Ghost Host lines for Haunted Mansion Holiday (2001) and for the 2003 film adaptation of the ride. Frees was married five times: to Anelle McCloud (1943–1945), Kleda June Hansen (1947–1950), Joyce Schultz (1951–divorced), Jeri J. Cole (1967–1969), and Beverly T. Marlow (1971–estranged at death). In his final two years, he suffered from arthritis, diabetes, and vision loss and endured constant pain; he died on November 2, 1986, at age 66 from a self-administered overdose of pain medication, with his death officially reported as suicide by his agent, who stated it was due to heart failure. His body was cremated, and his ashes were scattered over the Pacific Ocean.
